LaTeX
\paragraph{Driving Multiple Linkage Legs with One Motor.} For a linkage-driven walker, the legs must be spaced along the chassis to provide a sufficiently large support polygon. Mounting several identical four-bar mechanisms on the same crankshaft axis does not provide this longitudinal separation. Instead, one motor can drive multiple \emph{spatially separated crankshafts} using a timing belt, chain, or gear transmission. Each crankshaft operates its own four-bar walking leg, with the mechanisms positioned at the front, middle, and rear of the chassis. The crank angles can be offset to coordinate the stance and swing phases of different legs. For example, in a six-legged robot, the front and rear legs on one side can operate $180^\circ$ out of phase with the middle leg. This arrangement provides both spatial separation for stability and mechanical synchronization using fewer motors.

I've created a standalone interactive webpage for the two-DOF walking leg based on your Arduino sketch.

Two-DOF Walking Leg Simulator

Ready

Open or download the interactive HTML webpage

The webpage includes:

  • Hip angle slider: Adjust the hip servo from 30° to 150°.

  • Knee angle slider: Adjust the knee servo independently.

  • Live animation: Watch the thigh, knee, and foot move as you change the angles.

  • Play Arduino sequence: Animate the four movements from your original sketch.

  • Individual step buttons: Examine each movement separately.

  • Foot trajectory: Trace the movement of the foot.

  • Playback speed: Slow down or speed up the walking sequence.

How to use it

Download the HTML file and open it in Chrome or another browser. No installation or internet connection is required.

The simulator starts with both servos at 90°, matching your setup() function. Click Play Arduino sequence to see:

  1. Knee: 90° → 65° (lift)

  2. Hip: 90° → 110° (swing)

  3. Knee: 65° → 90° (lower)

  4. Hip: 110° → 90° (return)

One important teaching point: The simulation uses an assumed relationship between servo angle and leg angle. The actual direction of movement depends on how the servo horns are installed.

This would fit well in Module 8.6, where students transition from mechanically linked walking robots to independently controlled servo-driven legs.

I've updated the simulator so you can design leg positions using sliders, automatically generate Arduino commands, edit your own sketch, and play the resulting motion sequence.

Two-DOF Leg — Arduino Motion Playground

Download the interactive webpage (.html)

Your new workflow

  1. Set the hip and knee angles using the sliders and observe the leg position.

  2. Click Insert hip + knee + delay to add the selected pose to your Arduino sketch.

  3. Repeat to create a sequence of poses.

  4. Edit the generated Arduino code directly, including angles, variables, and delays.

  5. Click Play code to animate your sequence.

For example, setting hip to 110° and knee to 65° can insert:

C++
hip.write(110);
knee.write(65);
delay(350);

The webpage also includes playback speed control, pause, single-step execution, a foot trajectory trace, and a Download .ino option for using your sketch in Arduino IDE.

Important limitation: This is a motion visualizer rather than a full Arduino emulator. It supports Servo.write(), delay(), basic variables, and arithmetic. More complex constructs such as for loops, conditionals, and sensor-based control will produce an explicit unsupported-code message rather than an inaccurate animation.

I tested the sample sketch, insertion of custom slider angles, rebuilding the sequence, and playback in a browser.

You can publish the Two-DOF Leg Arduino Motion Playground on GitHub Pages for free. Since the simulator is a standalone HTML file, you don't need a web server, database, or additional software.

I recommend adding it to your existing GitHub Pages website as a separate interactive teaching tool.

Step 1: Download the HTML file

Download Two-DOF Leg Arduino Playground

Rename the file to:

index.html

Step 2: Upload it to your GitHub repository

  1. Go to GitHub and open the repository that hosts your website.

  2. Create a folder named two-dof-leg.

  3. Open that folder and select Add file → Upload files.

  4. Upload the renamed index.html.

  5. Click Commit changes.

Your repository structure should look something like this:

your-github-pages-repository/

index.html (your existing homepage)

two-dof-leg/

index.html (new simulator)

Step 3: Make sure GitHub Pages is enabled

In your repository, navigate to Settings → Pages.

Under Build and deployment, choose:

  • Source: Deploy from a branch

  • Branch: main (or your existing publishing branch)

  • Folder: / (root)

Click Save, if needed. If your existing website already works, leave its publishing settings unchanged.

GitHub Docs

Step 4: Open the simulator on your website

If your existing website is:

https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/

then the simulator will be available at:

https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/two-dof-leg/

If your website is hosted in a project repository, such as:

https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/REPOSITORY/

the simulator will be at:

https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/REPOSITORY/two-dof-leg/

The site should become accessible after GitHub Pages completes deployment.

Step 5: Add a link to your existing website

You can add the following HTML wherever you want students to find the simulator:

HTML
<a href="/two-dof-leg/" target="_blank">
  Interactive Two-DOF Walking Leg Simulator
</a>

For a project website hosted under /REPOSITORY/, use href="two-dof-leg/" or the full URL instead.

Optional: Embed the simulator within your course page

You could also embed the interactive simulator directly into a webpage:

HTML
<iframe
  src="two-dof-leg/"
  width="100%"
  height="850"
  style="border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 8px;"
  title="Two-DOF Walking Leg Simulator">
</iframe>

Students would then be able to adjust the hip and knee angles, build their Arduino sequence, and play the motion without leaving your course website.

For MEC101, I recommend hosting it as a standalone page and linking to it from Module 8.6. That gives students plenty of screen space to view the mechanism and edit Arduino code side by side.
